Title: Cost, reduced regional allowance deter doctors from Sabah, Sarawak postings
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Cost of living and a reduction in regional allowances following the implementation of the Public Service Remuneration System (SSPA) are among the factors believed to be discouraging some medical officers from accepting postings in Sabah and Sarawak.
Hartal Doktor Kontrak (HDK) spokesman Dr Muhammad Yassin said some doctors were even willing to reject offers of permanent appointments if they were posted to either state.
He said permanent appointments were not offered regularly, and rejecting one could affect a doctor's career prospects.
"Many do not want to go because of the cost, especially those who are already married.
"With the SSPA system, regional allowances have been reduced, and this has become one of the considerations for doctors when they are offered postings in Sabah or Sarawak," he told Berita Harian.
It was previously reported that several hospitals in Sabah and Sarawak were facing a shortage of medical officers after allegedly having no new doctors report for permanent appointments this month.
https://www.nst.com.my/news/regional/2026/10/1545319/sabah-hospitals-face-doctor-shortage-amid-low-turnout-new-mos
The Health Ministry has not disclosed the actual number of medical officers who failed to report for duty, although social media users had raised claims of medical officers "missing" from their respective postings.
Dr Muhammad said the regional allowance was previously 12.5 per cent of a doctor's monthly salary, but under the SSPA, the payment had been incorporated into the Regional Incentive Payment.
He said this had indirectly reduced the financial appeal for doctors who had to relocate far from the peninsula, particularly those with families who faced additional costs such as accommodation and travel.
"If the Federal Government or the Sabah and Sarawak governments could provide additional incentives, they might be more willing to go there," he said.
Doctors urged to weigh options
Dr Muhammad said the issue needed attention as permanent appointments were not offered continuously to all contract doctors, with some receiving only one opportunity during their service.
He said contract doctors who failed to receive an offer of a permanent appointment or a new contract after a certain period might have to move to the private sector to continue their careers.
"After seven years, if they are not offered another appointment, they will have to move to clinics or the private sector.
"That seven-year period includes two years of housemanship, meaning they have about another five years of service," he said.
He said this meant some doctors had to carefully consider a posting, including whether the benefits offered were worth the costs and implications for their family lives.
On action against doctors who failed to report for their offered postings, Malaysian Medical Association president Dr Sivanaesan Letchumanan said the reasons behind their decision should first be understood.
He said taking action without addressing the root causes could result in more doctors leaving the public healthcare system, which was already facing a shortage of manpower.
"Taking action without addressing the root causes risks causing more doctors to leave the public healthcare system, which is already short of manpower," he told BH yesterday.
He said the priority now should be to ensure the postings offered were attractive enough to encourage doctors to accept them and remain in the public service.

Title: Magnitude 6.1, 5.9 quakes strike Indonesia's Sumba, Aceh
Article:
JAKARTA: Two earthquakes measuring 6.1 and 5.9 in magnitude struck Indonesia's Sumba Island and Aceh province respectively this morning, with tremors felt across several areas.
The country's Meteorology, Climatology and Geophysics Agency (BMKG) said the magnitude 6.1 quake struck at 5.55am local time, with its epicentre at sea, about 14 kilometres southwest of Kodi in Southwest Sumba, East Nusa Tenggara province, at a depth of 10 kilometres.
According to data published on its website, the tremors were strongly felt in West Sumba and West Manggarai, with shaking also reported in East Sumba and Manggarai.
About 42 minutes later, the agency said the magnitude 5.9 quake struck at 6.37am, with its epicentre at sea, about 68 kilometres southwest of Calang in Aceh province at a depth of 26 kilometres.
BMKG said tremors from the second quake were felt in several parts of Aceh, including Aceh Besar, Banda Aceh, West Aceh, South Aceh, Pidie Jaya, Bener Meriah, Nagan Raya and Central Aceh.
The agency advised residents in the affected areas to remain alert for possible aftershocks.
There were no immediate reports of casualties or damage from either earthquake. — BERNAMA

Title: Three male students held over death of Form Four girl
Article:
BATU PAHAT: Three 16-year-old male students were arrested yesterday to assist investigations into the death of a Form Four girl whose body was found in a school hall in Yong Peng here.
The three were detained several hours after the body of Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairool Faisal, 16, was discovered at about 5.30pm.
A source said one of the students is expected to be brought before the Batu Pahat Magistrate's Court this morning to seek a remand order.
The three are students at the same school as the victim.
Irene Sofiya's body
was found by her grandmother, who had gone to the school after the girl failed to return home.
Police are investigating the case as murder.

Title: True meaning of a successful workplace
Article:
LETTERS:
A workplace is not truly successful simply because it produces more, earns more or achieves its targets. A truly successful workplace is one where people can return home safely and in good health at the end of every working day.
Accidents  can be caused  by chemicals, electricity, working at heights and vehicles.
Others are less visible — fatigue, stress, excessive workloads, poor ergonomics, bullying, harassment and other psychosocial risks.
Whether we work in a factory, construction site, office, hospital, school, warehouse, plantation or government department, risks exist.
The question is not whether accidents can happen. The question is: what are we doing to prevent them?
An accident is rarely simply "an accident". Behind many incidents are unsafe conditions, inadequate training, poor supervision, fatigue, weak communication or failure to learn from previous incidents.
This is why prevention must come before reaction. We must identify hazards, assess risks and control them before someone gets hurt.
Safety inspections, risk assessments, maintenance, safe operating procedures, training, personal protective equipment and emergency preparedness are not bureaucratic requirements.
They are life-saving measures. Too often, organisations become serious about safety only after something goes wrong.
By then, someone may have suffered serious injury, permanent disability or even death.
A family may have lost its breadwinner. A business may suffer lost productivity, compensation costs, legal consequences and reputational damage.
We must therefore build a culture that prevents accidents rather than merely investigates them afterwards.
Safety cannot be left solely to the safety officer or safety and health committee.
Management must provide leadership. Supervisors must provide proper guidance. Workers must follow safe work practices and speak up when they see hazards.
Contractors and subcontractors must meet the same safety standards. Safety is a shared responsibility — but leadership must come from the top.
If management treats safety as a genuine priority, that commitment will influence the entire organisation.
We must create workplaces where workers feel safe to report hazards, near misses and unsafe practices without fear of blame or punishment.
Workplace health is not only about physical injuries. Mental health matters too.
Stress, burnout, excessive workloads, bullying, harassment and other psychosocial risks can seriously affect a person's wellbeing and performance.
Some workers may be suffering silently. We need workplaces where people can seek help without stigma or fear.
A healthy worker is not simply someone who is free from physical injury. It is someone who is physically and mentally able to work safely and effectively.
Safety should not be viewed merely as a cost. It is an investment.
Preventing accidents reduces medical and compensation costs, equipment damage, production losses and reputational harm.
More importantly, it prevents human suffering. A safe workplace can improve morale, productivity, employee retention and confidence.
Safety and productivity are not opposing goals. Safety supports sustainable productivity.
We must also take near misses seriously. A near miss is a warning — an opportunity to prevent a more serious accident.
Instead of saying, "Nothing happened," we should ask, "What could have happened, and what must we do to ensure it does not happen?"
Workers should be encouraged to report near misses and hazards. The objective should be to identify root causes and prevent recurrence, not simply to find someone to blame.
Ultimately, safety is about culture. Rules and regulations are necessary, but rules alone cannot create a safe workplace.
We need leadership, commitment and accountability. Every manager should regularly ask:
Are our workers properly trained? Are risks properly assessed and controlled? Are safety procedures actually being followed?
Can workers report hazards without fear? Are contractors meeting the required standards? And are we learning from accidents and near misses?
The workplace is also changing rapidly through automation, artificial intelligence, new technologies, flexible working arrangements and changing workforce demographics.
New technology should not merely make work faster. It should make work safer.
We must use technology to identify hazards, improve training, strengthen emergency response and reduce workers' exposure to dangerous tasks.
At the end of the day, workplace safety is about people. Behind every worker is a family. Behind every injury is a human story.
And behind every workplace fatality is a family whose life may never be the same again.
We must therefore move:
From reacting to accidents to preventing them.
From compliance to commitment.
From blame to learning.
From silence to speaking up.
And from seeing safety as a cost to recognising it as an investment in people and the future of our organisations.
Let every worker know: "My life matters. My health matters. My safety matters."
And let every employer understand: "Every accident we prevent is a life we protect."
The true measure of a successful workplace is not simply how much it produces, but how well it protects the people who make that success possible.
TAN SRI LEE LAM THYE
Safety advocate
Kuala Lumpur
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: 5.8-Magnitude earthquake strikes North Sumatra — MetMalaysia
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A moderate earthquake measuring 5.8 on the Richter scale was detected in North Sumatra, Indonesia at 7.37am today.

Title: Ringgit expected to gain ground next week amid weaker US job data
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The ringgit is expected to strengthen against the US dollar next week, trading in the range of RM4.07 to RM4.08, as weaker-than-expected US employment data could reinforce expectations that the US Federal Reserve might skip a rate hike this month.
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid told Bernama that the latest US labour market data could weigh on the greenback and provide support for the ringgit.
He pointed out that US non-farm payrolls (NFP) rose by only 29,000 jobs in September, well below market expectations of 89,000, while the unemployment rate increased to 4.2 per cent.
Mohd Afzanizam said the focus next week would be on the tabling of Malaysia's Budget 2027 on Oct 9, with market participants likely to assess the government's fiscal deficit target for 2027 and whether there would be any adjustment to this year's deficit target of 3.5 per cent of gross domestic product (GDP).
He said the government's total revenue grew 12 per cent to RM165.4 billion in the first half of 2026, driven mainly by a 32 per cent increase in sales and service tax collection.
However, operating expenditure rose 14.4 per cent to RM94.6 billion, underpinned by a 61.2 per cent increase in subsidies to RM38.0 billion during the period, he noted.
"In this regard, market participants will be observing the macroeconomic targets, such as GDP, inflation and the fiscal deficit for 2027 given that external risks remain fairly visible next year," he added.
Meanwhile, on a Friday-to-Friday basis, the ringgit weakened against the greenback to 4.0820/0870 from 4.0715/0765 a week earlier.
The local currency traded mostly lower against a basket of other major currencies during the week.
It strengthened to 4.5927/5983 versus the euro from 4.6378/6435 in the previous Friday.
However, the ringgit depreciated against the British pound to 5.3927/3993 from 5.3907/3973 a week earlier and fell vis-a-vis the Japanese yen to 2.5906/5941 from 2.5764/5797 previously.
It traded mixed against ASEAN currencies.
The local note slipped versus the Singapore dollar to 3.1908/1952 from 3.1858/1900 a week earlier and weakened against the Indonesian rupiah to 228.2/228.6 from 227.4/227.8.
In contrast, it appreciated vis-a-vis the Thai baht to 12.1579/1778 from 12.2036/2234 at the end of last week and was little changed against the Philippine peso to 6.52/6.54 from 6.52/6.53 previously.

Title: Bursa Malaysia key index seen in the 1,620-1,650 range next week
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Bursa Malaysia's key index is expected to hover within the 1,620-1,650 range next week, with selective accumulation of quality blue-chip stocks likely to emerge on weakness, said an analyst.
Rakuten Trade Sdn Bhd vice-president of equity research Thong Pak Leng said the 1,620 area should serve as the immediate support zone, while a recovery above 1,650 could pave the way towards 1,660.
"A stronger move beyond 1,660 would improve the near-term technical picture, although a more sustainable recovery would still require easing bond yields, greater stability in crude oil prices and stronger participation from index heavyweights," he told Bernama.
For the trading week ended yesterday, profit-taking and selling pressure dominated early trading, while the subsequent sharp sell-off prompted bargain hunting as the market entered oversold conditions.
On a Friday-to-Friday basis, the FTSE Bursa Malaysia KLCI (FBM KLCI) dropped 40.75 points to 1,630.87 at yesterday's close from 1,671.62 a week earlier.
On the index board, the FBM Emas Index decreased 286.07 points to 12,170.57, the FBM Top 100 Index fell 285.78 points to 11,957.68, the FBM Emas Shariah Index shed 245.91 points to 12,060.32, the FBM ACE Index inched down 3.40 points to 5,529.46, and the FBM Mid 70 Index slid 362.98 points to 17,481.93.
By sector, the Energy Index slipped 28.80 points to 833.03, the Plantation Index erased 278.32 points to 9,056.55, the Industrial Products and Services Index shaved off 5.58 points to 178.52, and the Financial Services Index trimmed 509.98 points to 19,040.51.
Weekly turnover firmed to 17.39 billion units worth RM14.42 billion from 17.11 billion units worth RM14.07 billion in the previous week.

Title: Student found dead in school hall was top student, tipped for 9As, says classmate
Article:
BATU PAHAT: Form Four student Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairool Faisal, 16, was among her school's top students and was seen as a strong candidate to score straight As in next year's Sijil Pelajaran Malaysia (SPM), said her classmate.
The classmate, who declined to be named, said Irene Sofiya was absent from an extra class yesterday, but her friends initially assumed she was unwell.
"During the extra class yesterday, she was not in class. We thought she was absent because she was not feeling well.
She added a teacher asked about Irene Sofiya, but the students did not know why she was absent.
"I only found out later that Irene Sofiya had not returned home. I did not think anything bad had happened to her," the student said when met.
The student said some female students had suspected something was wrong but did not provide further details.
Later, a teacher contacted the students individually to ask when their extra classes had started and ended after Maghrib.
"I was puzzled and asked the teacher about it. The teacher eventually told us that something 'bad' had happened at the school that day.
"I was shocked and never expected something like this to happen," the student said.
The classmate described Irene Sofiya as a focused student who was also active in school activities.
"She was one of the best students in the school and had the potential to score straight As in the SPM next year.
"She was focused on her studies and active in school activities. That is why we still cannot believe what happened to her.
"We can still picture her face and never imagined we would lose her," the student said.
In the incident at about 5.30pm yesterday, Irene Sofiya was found dead with injuries to her body, believed to have been murdered inside the hall of a secondary school in Yong Peng.
She was found by her grandmother and a friend who went to the school after realising that she had not returned home despite her extra class having ended.
Irene Sofiya was understood to have been living with her grandmother after her mother died of cancer some time ago, while her father works in Kuala Lumpur.
Blood stains were found on her body, along with bruises believed to have been caused by blows.
A broken flower pot was also found near the victim.

Title: School murder: Grandmother holds dying granddaughter, helps her recite the syahadah
Article:
BATU PAHAT: A Form Four student who was found severely injured at a secondary school in Yong Peng here yesterday managed to raise her hand and turn towards her grandmother in what would be their final moments together.
Irene Sofiya Mohd Khairool Faisal, 16, or 'Fiya' to her friends and family, was found in the school hall with severe injuries believed to have been inflicted with a hard object.
Her grandmother, Jameyah Rabani, 65, said Fiya's friend found her in a pool of blood and called for her to enter the hall.
"I ran to her... it was  heartbreaking. Fiya could no longer speak, but she raised her hand and turned to look at me.
"I hugged Fiya and helped her recite the syahadah," she said when met at her home in Kampung Parit Selamat, Yong Peng, today.
Jameyah said Fiya became unresponsive when she called her name several times.
She said before Fiya was found, two of her friends had gone to her house to ask whether she had returned home after they found her motorcycle inside the school compound.
"Yesterday, Fiya attended an extra class from 2pm to about 5pm.
"Her friends came to ask whether she had returned home. I told them she had not.
"I became worried and asked my daughter (Siti Nur Faeza Khyar, 45), and Fiya's friends to look for her around the school.
"We searched for some time but could not find her. Then one of her friends screamed and told me she had found Fiya covered in blood," she said.
Jameyah said she had invited Fiya to attend a wedding yesterday morning, but her granddaughter couldn't as she had an online extra class at 11am and another class at school at 2pm.
"I accept what has happened, but I am deeply saddened. We have lost her. My husband and I raised her from the age of nine after her mother died of cancer," she said.
Meanwhile, Fiya's grandfather, Khyar Abas, 69, said he never expected their conversation over breakfast that morning to be their last.
He said he and his aunt, who had come from Kluang, had waited for Fiya to go out for a meal, but she never returned from school.
"We lived together, just the three of us. She was never a source of worry and was a diligent student," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Protests over housing flare in Spain after relief measures rejected
Article:
MADRID, (Spain): Tens of thousands of protesters marched in Madrid and other cities in Spain on Saturday to demand affordable housing, a day after lawmakers rejected relief measures for tenants.
The demonstrations extended a crisis that has gone on for more than a week, triggered by the eviction last month of a pensioner, 87-year-old Maricarmen Abascal, from her Madrid flat.
The defeat was another political setback for Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez and has renewed questions over whether his minority government can survive until the next scheduled general election in 2027.
His government's proposed measures, which included automatic renewal of tenancy contracts and restrictions on evicting vulnerable tenants, were voted down by opposition parties on Friday in Spain's parliament.
The defeat infuriated those protesting the country's increasingly expensive housing market.
Hundreds of protesters have been occupying a tent city set up a week ago in the heart of Madrid to press for reforms.
Late on Saturday groups of far-right protesters, some of them performing Nazi salutes, tried to get to the camp but were blocked by police.
One video posted on the website of Spanish daily El Pais showed police chasing some members of the group through the streets and the newspaper also reported that officers had made three arrests.
- General strike call -
Earlier Saturday, demonstrators marched through the capital's streets. Authorities said 70,000 people participated, but the organisers put the figure at 500,000.
Smaller demonstrations took place in other cities, including Palma de Mallorca, Santander, Segovia and Toledo.
In Valencia, five people were arrested after clashes with police, local media reported.
At the Madrid protest Marcos Sainz, a librarian of 26, said he used to rent a two-bedroom apartment with friends for a total monthly rent of 900 euros ($1,000).
Today, a one-bedroom flat often costs 1,000 euros — or half the median monthly salary in the capital, he told AFP.
He would protest rental spikes "until someone dares to regulate it all as (otherwise) we'll all have to leave Madrid and that would be a shame as I am from Madrid."
"We are demanding a fundamental right," said Javier, a 31-year-old solar panel installer. "Decent housing, stability and conditions allowing us to construct a decent life project.
"I spend half of my salary on a tiny room," he added.
Valeria Racu, one of the spokespeople of the Tenants' Union organising the protest, said in a statement that the last eight days' protests had shown the effectiveness of people's power.
"Now begins real politics — politics which has always belonged to the people and which will return once and for all to the streets," she added.
She repeated her union's call for a general strike.
- Calls for early election -
Housing has for years been a top concern for Spaniards as supply falls short of demand, with rents and house prices rising as elsewhere in the European Union.
Average rents in Spain have almost doubled over the past decade, while asking prices for homes have risen by about 90 percent, according to real estate website Idealista.
Abascal's eviction catalysed long-running anger about runaway housing costs.
The pensioner was forced to leave the Madrid flat where she had lived for more than seven decades after it was acquired by an investment company that sought to increase her rent by 275 per cent, say housing campaigners.
The backlash led the property's new owners to reach a deal allowing her to return to the flat at a low rent.
The housing bills Sanchez's leftist coalition had presented to parliament were rejected after the Catalan separatist party Junts — on whose support the government relies — voted against them, arguing they lacked rigour.
Junts joined the main opposition Popular Party (PP) and the far-right Vox party in shooting down the measures.
PP leader Alberto Nunez Feijoo on Saturday urged Sanchez to call early elections "because the country can't take any more."
Recent opinion polls have generally placed the Popular Party ahead of the Socialists. — AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Crash investigators check 800 motor cases yearly
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Field checks remain the most vital tool in detecting fraudulent motor insurance claims despite advancing technology, said a loss-adjusting firm that handles over 800 cases nationwide every year.
General Adjustment Expertise Sdn Bhd investigation manager Jegatheesan Balakrishnan said each investigator handles about 65 motor cases a month.
Of these, eight to 10 cases involve false or exaggerated claims, he said.
He said 16 investigators handle the cases, comprising four who specialise in car accident investigations and 12 who handle bodily injury claims.
He said the cases included fraudulent or staged damage, ranging from simple "parked and damaged" incidents involving false police reports to complex, staged multi-vehicle collisions.
"In simple cases, motorists hit obstacles such as metal railings or trees and later lodge false reports claiming their vehicles were struck by other vehicles. After checking, we can see that the damage patterns are different," he said.
"In more complicated setups, syndicates or third parties deliberately stage accidents using pre-damaged or mechanically defective vehicles to file fraudulent claims."
[[nid:1547147]]
Jegatheesan said some workshops had contributed to fraudulent claims by adding old, pre-existing damage, such as side or rear dents, to a single front-end collision claim.
"Sometimes a workshop will include pre-existing damage. For example, they may claim the vehicle was rear-ended by another vehicle.
"So basically, the damage should be at the rear, but sometimes they will include damage on all sides, left, right and front. In such cases, the damage is inconsistent and requires further investigation."
He said their investigators regularly visit accident scenes for a better understanding of the incidents rather than relying on photos and reports.
"Part of the job is to inspect accident sites, verify impact measurements against vehicle damage, check the surroundings, CCTV footage and interview nearby residents or business operators."
Jegatheesan, who has 20 years of industry experience, said modern vehicle technology, such as post-crash assistance systems and dashcams, provides crucial objective evidence, but artificial intelligence presents new challenges.
"AI makes evidence far easier to tamper with, including manipulated scene photographs and falsified timestamps. That is why taking statements, conducting interviews and detailed chronological cross-checking by investigators are essential."
He said safety features in newer vehicles help facilitate post-crash assistance when motorists call for roadside services.
"So from there, we can gather the information. Dashcams are also helpful because they can be used to identify accidents. This will help us in our investigations to detect any untoward incidents."
Jegatheesan said inflated costs from workshops and disputes over repair costs had drastically reduced.
This, he said, was due to Bank Negara Malaysia's centralised database under the Motor Data Research Consortium Malaysia, which standardised spare part pricing and labour hours directly from car manufacturers.

Title: Fraudulent claims cannot justify higher premiums, say consumer groups
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Consumers should not be unfairly burdened due to fraudulent or manipulated motor insurance claims, the Federation of Malaysian Consumers Associations (Fomca) said.
Fomca chief executive officer Dr T. Saravanan said the reality was that rising claims costs would eventually affect insurance premiums.
"For now, there may be regulatory controls and safeguards," he said.
"But how long can consumers continue to be protected if the underlying problems within the industry are not addressed?"
He said it was time to revamp the motor insurance claims ecosystem as the present framework clearly needed stronger checks and balances.
"Similar to efforts to reset and reform the healthcare and medical insurance ecosystem, we need a comprehensive review of the motor insurance industry, particularly the claims process."
He said Fomca's approach was not merely to receive complaints, but to help consumers understand the issue, identify the parties involved and facilitate dispute resolution where appropriate through the National Consumer Complaints Centre.
"The first step is usually to obtain the relevant documents and evidence and engage the company, insurer, workshop or other relevant party to seek clarification and an appropriate resolution."
He said there was a need to establish a neutral and independent mechanism to verify questionable or high-value claims.
"When different parties within the ecosystem have their own commercial interests, there is always a risk of conflict of interest, inflated costs or weaknesses being exploited.
"Ultimately, these additional costs may be passed back to consumers through higher premiums.
"Therefore, the responsibility cannot simply be placed on policyholders."
He said insurers must strengthen fraud detection and claims verification, while workshops, adjusters and other parties involved in fraudulent or inflated claims must also be held accountable.
Saravanan said Bank Negara Malaysia, as the regulator of the insurance industry, must take a firm lead in addressing these structural weaknesses.
"Insurance fraud should be investigated and tackled quickly, while the overall claims ecosystem should be reviewed to identify loopholes and strengthen accountability.
"This issue goes beyond motor insurance. Whether it involves motor, medical, personal or life insurance, continuously passing increasing costs back to consumers is not a sustainable solution.
"The emphasis must therefore be on reforming the system, closing loopholes, introducing stronger independent verification and taking firm action against fraud. Honest policyholders should not continually be made to pay for weaknesses and abuses within the system."
The Malaysia Consumers Movement (MCM) said policyholders should not be forced to bear the burden of higher insurance premiums based on unsubstantiated allegations of motor insurance fraud.
MCM legal adviser Mohan Sankaran said genuine policyholders who strictly abide by their policy terms should not collectively absorb industry losses attributed to unverified or merely suspected fraud.
"Consumers should not be made to bear the cost of fraud through higher premiums as a matter of course. If insurers believe a claim is fraudulent or manipulated, then that claim must be properly investigated and supported by evidence."
[[nid:1547143]]
'STRONGER FRAUD DETECTION MUST COME FIRST'
He said the insurance industry must draw a clear line between suspected and established fraud and suspicion alone could not automatically classify a claim as fraudulent.
"Where fraud is proven, the appropriate action should be taken against the parties responsible.
"It would be unfair for genuine policyholders who have paid their premiums and complied with the terms of their policies to collectively absorb losses attributed to alleged fraud."
Mohan said insurance providers should prioritise tighter controls within their claims ecosystem and improve internal fraud detection mechanisms rather than passing financial burdens onto the public.
"The insurer's priority should therefore be stronger fraud detection, proper investigation, enforcement against offenders and tighter controls within the claims ecosystem rather than simply passing the financial burden on to consumers through higher premiums."
He added that any industry proposal seeking to justify premium hikes on the grounds of rising fraud must be backed by transparent, independently verifiable data showing the actual financial impact of proven fraudulent claims.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: AI needs safety layers like nuclear plants - ex-OpenAI engineer
Article:
NEW YORK: Another former OpenAI employee has added his voice to a chorus of frantic calls to make AI safe, saying the industry must mimic the aviation or nuclear power sectors with their layers of safeguards to avoid disaster.
In an article published in The Atlantic Magazine, David Robinson echoed warnings from inside and outside the AI world that its agents are being developed so fast and becoming so smart they could soon elude control and conceivably wipe out humanity.
Robinson said alarming incidents reported since the start of the summer – in which AI agents slipped out of their controlled spaces and went rogue to attack a variety of targets – show the industry is not taking safety nearly seriously enough as it sprints to develop faster and more powerful artificial intelligence capabilities.
In the essay Robinson said his credentials include overseeing the writing of safety reports on 12 advanced model product launches and leading the drafting of OpenAI's Preparedness Framework.
Robinson says he worked at OpenAI for three-and-a-half years and was among the longest-tenured employees at the company.
The mistakes revealed recently are typical because of "the speed and flexibility with which people operate," Robinson wrote.
He added: "An environment where things like this can happen is no place to grow artificial minds that could be smarter than we are and that might not do what we want them to."
He argued that cutting-edge AI labs need to operate like the aviation or the nuclear industry with layers of redundant safeguards and careful planning "so that the occasional and inevitable human error does not open a door to disaster."
Robinson also insisted that the issue of "alignment" – the industry term for how AI can be trained to respect human values – is essential but something the industry has failed to even define, much less master.
Then there's this, he said: AI models are getting better and better at detecting when they are being tested and might behave differently when they are actually deployed, fooling their masters.
After a meeting Tuesday at the White House, amid global worries about what AI means for humanity, top AI executives said they had committed to measures for self-regulation, as opposed to submitting to government rules. This includes internal controls on AI systems and bringing in outside analysts.
President Donald Trump is vehemently against government regulation of AI and insists that criticism that AI is dangerous is just a "hoax."
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Taman Sri Muda flood victims staying vigilant
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Residents of Taman Sri Muda, Shah Alam, have not experienced severe flooding since the disastrous December 2021 incident, but they are not letting their guard down.
Thinash Kumar Nair, 43, a
cybersecurity firm sales director who has lived in the area for 14 years, said the sight of his double-storey home being inundated was traumatic.
[[nid:1547252]]
"Even though there have been no  floods as bad as that over the last few years, every  time it rains heavily, the fear returns.
"My family gets anxious and we automatically move our cars to higher ground.
"We also keep emergency bags in our vehicles just to be safe," he told the
New Straits Times
.
Recalling the tragedy, Thinash said he lost all household contents, including furniture and electronics, and two vehicles.
"It struck 11 months after I spent RM100,000 renovating my house, bringing the total loss to between RM180,000 and RM220,000.
"We were left with nothing except the clothes on our backs.
"After the incident, we only received RM1,000 in government aid and another RM1,000 voucher from a Buddhist charity organisation."
On Tuesday, 50 residents won a suit against the government and several public authorities over the devastating floods.
High Court judicial commissioner Shoba Rajah Dorai Rajah found the defendants fully liable for negligence and related failures.
The residents had sued the government and seven others, claiming that failures in flood management, drainage, weather warnings and disaster response contributed to their losses.
Thinash described the verdict as a crucial step toward public accountability, but added that no monetary compensation could fully restore what was lost.
"I won't say I'm happy, but it is satisfying to know that someone is finally taking responsibility for what happened.
"The money is immaterial. No matter how much they pay, it won't bring back what we lost."
Another resident, Pirakas Sabapathy, 35, said his family lost about RM10,000.
[[nid:1547251]]
"I only grabbed some of my daughter's clothes and the computer I needed for work.
"Within a few hours, the water was too high and we lost hope. We just prayed for the rain to stop."
He said his wife, mother and then 1-year-old daughter could only watch as floods destroyed everything on the ground level.
The floods damaged doors, staircase structures and household appliances, including the refrigerator, television and washing machine.
He said while the drainage and riverbank repairs over the last two years had prevented severe recurring floods, heavy downpours still trigger anxiety.
"My mother and grandmother still have that phobia.
"Whenever it rains heavily at night, they cannot sleep without leaving all the lights on.
"Even now, we keep all our essential belongings and clothes on the second floor."
He said they were happy with the court's decision and it showed that they could still get fair compensation.
​Pirakas hoped the state authorities would accept the court's judgment without lengthy appeals, noting that formal assistance arrived far too late during the 2021 disaster.
Their lawyer, James Joshua Paulraj, said the judgment was an important vindication for the residents of Taman Sri Muda, who waited nearly five years for accountability.
"The court recognised that extreme rainfall does not absolve public authorities of their operational responsibilities when reasonable preparation, timely warnings and an effective disaster response could have reduced the harm suffered."
He said the lessons of this disaster must translate into effective measures to prevent residents from suffering the same consequences again.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: RM1b lost yearly to fraud, say adjusters
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Fraudulent motor insurance claims account for an estimated RM1 billion in losses annually, said insurance adjusters.
Association of Malaysian Loss Adjusters (AMLA) chairman Y.K. Foo said the most prevalent fraudulent claims involved accidents, vehicle thefts, fires and staged collisions.
"While the majority of claims submitted to insurers are genuine, fraud remains a persistent issue," he said.
Foo said an adjusting firm could handle an average of 200 suspicious cases requiring formal investigation each year.
"Following thorough inquiries, approximately 40 to 50 per cent of these flagged cases are confirmed as actual, actionable fraud, with overall fraud incidence rates remaining relatively stable year on year."
He said AMLA had 41 members, nearly half of whom dealt with motor insurance fraud, while the rest handled other investigations and insurance claims.
Foo said the scams ranged from opportunistic individual policy breaches to highly organised syndicate operations.
"At the individual level, the most common tactic involves lapsed policies, in which vehicle owners who crash while uninsured quickly purchase a new policy before reporting the accident days later.
"Claims submitted within a week of renewing a long-lapsed policy are immediate red flags for investigators.
"Illegal operators sometimes pair an uninsured, damaged vehicle from a repair yard with an insured vehicle to stage a fake multi-vehicle crash and claim payouts on both.
"Another tactic involves faking or exaggerating personal injuries."
He said fraudsters previously preferred driving vehicles into monsoon drains, lakes or rivers to claim insurance, but a crackdown on those claims had prompted a shift towards vehicle arson.
"With fire, everything is destroyed and little evidence remains, apart from traces of accelerants."
He added that arson incidents had risen to around 20 cases annually per firm.
Foo also warned motorists against accident-scene touts who exploit drivers' panic to initiate fraudulent claims, with unscrupulous operators routinely towing vehicles to unapproved locations to cause secondary damage or re-impact them to inflate claim amounts.
"Everyone will be in a state of shock after an accident and may not know what to do. These unscrupulous people will tow your vehicle somewhere and probably tamper with the damage or bang the car again to inflate the claim amount."
To curb the issue in the long term, AMLA is advocating better information-sharing among insurers, adjusters, law enforcement agencies and medical institutions.
Foo added that if the entire ecosystem could develop a process through which legitimate claim information was shared quickly and securely, industry stakeholders could work together to reduce fraud and, ultimately, keep consumer premiums within a controlled percentage.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Storms, flooding cause chaos on Greek holiday island of Crete
Article:
ATHENS: Floods after heavy storms trapped some people in their cars and forced the evacuation of some tourists on the Greek holiday island of Crete, local officials said Saturday.
The force of the flooding washed some cars and trees into the sea.
"We had to evacuate a few tourists and a woman had to be taken to hospital as a precaution," the mayor of the Cretan port of Ierapetra, Manolis Frangoulis, told AFP.
The town, on the southeast coast of Crete, was hit by torrential rain Friday and Saturday, cutting off roads that had been filled with debris.
"We have cars in the sea and all the department is working to at least re-establish transport," Frangoulis.
On the road between Ierapetra and Sitia, flooding trapped 23 people in their cars, state television channel ERT reported.
Three tourists and their taxi driver had to abandon their vehicle after flood waters began to carry away their vehicle, ERT added.
At the port of Canea, a popular tourist destination, giant waves damaged seafront restaurants and tourist venues.
The civil protection agency called on residents of several towns to limit their movements.
The deputy governor of the Heraklion region, Nikos Syrigonakis, said emergency services were working to clear small landslides and remove debris from local roads.
They remained on high alert, monitoring the water levels of the streams and rivers, he told the Greek news agency ANA.
Between Friday and Saturday at 1550 GMT (6:50 pm), 42 cm of rain fell in the Canea department, said the Greek national observatory.
The wind speeds were reached up to eight and nine on the Beaufort Scale, said the EMY weather service.

Title: AI, digital forensics key tools to combat fake motor insurance claims
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysian general insurers have deployed advanced digital forensics, artificial intelligence and centralised tracking databases to combat organised crime syndicates and fake claims.
The General Insurance Association of Malaysia (PIAM) said the Fraud Intelligence System (FIS), managed by Insurance Services Malaysia, serves as the industry's primary database, allowing subscribing insurance companies to identify anomalies in claims.
PIAM chief executive officer Chua Kim Soon said insurers were using the FIS alongside new digital tools to counter sophisticated tactics, such as AI-edited crash photos and staged collisions.
"The system now uses specialised algorithms and software to analyse image pixels and metadata, instantly flagging fake photos or recycled images from older accidents," he said.
"To prevent the use of tampered photos, some of our insurance providers are also requesting drivers to submit crash photos through their own Digital Roadside Assistance mobile apps."
Chua said major insurers saved RM65 million between 2023 and last year by deploying the FIS to intercept dubious claims before payouts were made.
He said fraud scenarios ranged from opportunistic acts by individuals, such as exaggerating damage or colluding with third parties to falsify claims, to complex organised schemes involving multiple actors executing staged accidents, self-inflicted crashes, the use of private cars for commercial purposes or chain collisions.
The FIS received 924 fraudulent vehicle claim cases last year. Own damage, third-party bodily injury and third-party property damage were the most commonly reported claim types.
He said fraud investigations resulted in RM41 million in savings last year, up from RM21 million in 2024.
"The increase reflects higher case detection, strengthened validation processes and improved escalation of suspicious claims."
Chua said insurers also cross-verified claims against police reports, weather logs for flood claims and vehicle history databases before sending flagged cases to loss adjusters for physical vehicle inspections.
"Claims are cross-referenced using engine and chassis numbers and weather data, while cases involving suspected criminal syndicates are escalated to the police."
He added that cross-border smuggling had emerged as a critical concern, with commercial pickup trucks being 3.6 times more prone to theft than standard passenger cars.
"To combat these operations, which contributed to RM488 million in theft-related claims in 2025, insurers are partnering with the police and government agencies to monitor jungle borders where stolen high-clearance vehicles are routinely trafficked into Thailand and Indonesia."
He added that insurers also worked with government and non-government bodies to reduce vehicle theft and road accidents. An independent panel of loss adjusters supported these efforts by conducting mandatory interviews, crime scene inspections, travel log checks and financial background audits to verify high-risk theft claims.
At the same time, the insurance industry actively participates in anti-fraud dialogues, sends teams for specialised training and joins executive roundtables to strengthen industry-wide defences.
These platforms allow organisations to share practical threat intelligence, discuss emerging schemes and stay ahead of fraud trends.
Continuous training ensures operational teams can quickly identify red flags, while executive roundtables help leadership align on unified mitigation strategies, which fosters cross-industry collaboration to protect consumers from fraud.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Motor insurance fraud on the rise [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Motor insurance fraud cases have surged dramatically over the past three years, driven by evolving syndicate tactics, opportunistic financial schemes and the misuse of digital image manipulation tools to exploit claims processes.
General Insurance Association of Malaysia (PIAM) chief executive officer Chua Kim Soon said the motor insurance industry was operating at a loss as total premiums collected fall short of insurance costs.
He said fraudulent activity had worsened the financial losses of 19 general insurers who are members of PIAM, which recorded an underwriting loss of RM289.3 million last year.
"As many as 10 per cent of all motor insurance claims filed with Malaysian insurers are potentially fraudulent or manipulated, resulting in financial losses of hundreds of millions of ringgit," he said.
"This leakage directly harms honest policyholders as insurance companies are ultimately forced to adjust overall premium rates to absorb the deficit."
He added that 924 fraudulent cases were reported last year, up from 425 in 2024 and 68 in 2023.
[[nid:1547190]]
"This means that total claims payouts and operational expenditure have consistently exceeded total premiums collected."
He said fraudulent scenarios ranged from opportunistic acts by individual vehicle owners, such as exaggerating repair damage or swapping driver identities, to highly sophisticated organised criminal schemes involving staged multi-vehicle collisions and fake total-loss payouts.
Chua added that insurers were also increasingly dealing with cases involving unauthorised or unlicensed drivers, private vehicles being illegally used for commercial hire and driving under the influence.
"While insurance companies have the legal right to reject such claims under standard policy exclusions, cases involving policyholders who file false police reports to conceal the true circumstances of an incident are classified as criminal fraud. Such acts may constitute cheating and criminal breach of trust under Malaysian law."
He said industry data also highlighted disparities in claims behaviour between Peninsular Malaysia and Sabah and Sarawak.
"Peninsular Malaysia recorded a significantly higher claim frequency of 5.1 per cent, compared with 1.7 per cent in Sabah and Sarawak.
"But motor claims in Sabah and Sarawak can run substantially higher, averaging RM12,000. Accidents occur less frequently but result in costlier own-damage claims."
He said repair costs were becoming more expensive, particularly for imported spare parts used in foreign and high-end vehicle models, with motor repair costs recording a compound annual growth rate of 7.9 per cent between 2021 and 2025.
On court awards, Chua said average personal injury compensation had trended upward.
Historically, he said, major bodily injury awards were about RM600,000, but they now frequently exceed RM1 million, while extreme cases could reach RM8 million.
Chua said insurers cross-check through the Fraud Intelligence System alongside investigations by loss adjusters to combat fraud.
"Claims could also be cross-referenced using engine and chassis numbers and weather data. Cases involving suspected criminal syndicates are escalated to the police."
The New Straits Times has reached out to the police for their input.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Melaka polls: PH-Bersatu pact may boost chances against BN
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A potential electoral cooperation between Pakatan Harapan and Bersatu could strengthen both parties' prospects in the Melaka election by helping the coalition shore up Malay support and giving Bersatu a broader platform.
Political analysts said this could prevent a split in votes and enable PH and Bersatu to mount a stronger challenge against Barisan Nasional, which has emerged from recent state elections with strong results.
They said the biggest hurdle would be convincing PH grassroots to accept Bersatu, given the latter's role in the political upheaval that led to the collapse of the PH administration during the Sheraton Move in 2020.
Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities director Associate Professor Dr Mazlan Ali said the proposed cooperation could give PH a stronger platform to challenge BN, particularly as PH continued to face difficulties in securing Malay support.
He said PH's performance in recent state elections highlighted the importance of bringing additional Malay support into any broader electoral arrangement, while Bersatu needed to work with a larger coalition to remain competitive.
"PH, after the Johor and Negri Sembilan elections, found that it lacked Malay support.
"And Bersatu, after being sidelined by Pas, is on its own.
"Ber-satu cannot contest alone and needs to join a larger coalition."
BN won 48 of the 56 seats in the Johor election in July.
In the following month, it won 18 of the 36 seats in Negri Sembilan, with Perikatan Nasional taking  seven.
Mazlan said Bersatu could provide PH with more support among Malay voters, while PH could give Bersatu a platform to remain electorally competitive.
He said this could be significant in mixed constituencies, where the combination of Malay and non-Malay support could allow PH and Bersatu to mount a stronger challenge.
[[nid:1547173]]
"For Bersatu, there is no other option. BN will not accept it and Pas has already removed the party (from PN).
"What Bersatu has now is PH."
Mazlan said the proposed cooperation should not be viewed as unusual despite the history between the two parties.
"In politics, there are no permanent enemies and no permanent friends.
"What matters is how both parties can use the situation to strengthen their position."
International Islamic University Malaysia political analyst and Ishak Institute fellow Associate Professor Dr Syaza Shukri said the proposed cooperation was realistic as PH and Bersatu were at a point where they had little to lose by exploring a new arrangement.
"But the problem is whether the grassroots, especially those in PH, can accept Bersatu, which is seen as having betrayed PH."
Syaza said the cooperation could make the contest more competitive by creating an almost one-to-one contest between the opposing sides, should BN and PN work together.
She said a split in votes between PH and Bersatu could make it easier for BN to secure victories, whereas cooperation could prevent opposition votes from being divided.
Syaza said the cooperation alone might not be enough for PH and Bersatu to secure 15 seats, the simple majority needed to form the government.
She said its immediate effect would instead be to make the contest more competitive.
The potential  cooperation comes as the two sides continue discussions on a possible electoral arrangement for the  election.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: 16-year-old student found dead at Yong Peng school [WATCH]
Article:
BATU PAHAT: A 16-year-old Form Four student was found dead with injuries at a secondary school in Yong Peng here this afternoon, in what is suspected to be a murder.
The victim was found by her grandmother, who went to the school after becoming concerned when her granddaughter had not returned home by about 5.30pm.
According to a source, the victim lived with her grandmother after her mother died, while her father worked in Kuala Lumpur.
The source said the grandmother rushed to the school to look for her before finding the girl lying weak and unresponsive.
"Dried blood was found on the victim's body, along with bruises that appeared to be from being beaten. A broken flowerpot was also found near the victim," the source said.
Meanwhile, Batu Pahat district police chief Assistant Commissioner Shahrulanuar Mushaddat Abdullah Sani said investigations were ongoing.
"Police are investigating the incident before issuing any statement," he said.
A check at the scene found members of the public, including students from the school, gathered outside the school gates to follow developments.
A forensic team from the Johor police contingent headquarters was also seen at the school hall collecting evidence.
The school's main entrance was tightly guarded, with only security personnel and authorised parties allowed to enter.

Title: Full relocation allowance for doctors posted to Sabah, Sarawak
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The Health Ministry has approved full relocation allowances for medical officers posted to Sabah and Sarawak to support their welfare and facilitate cross-regional placements.
In a statement today, the ministry said the approval was among its strategic initiatives to ensure financial constraints no longer burden health workers receiving postings across regions.
"The government is deeply concerned about the financial challenges faced by health workers.
"With the approval of the Finance Ministry and Public Service Department (PSD), the issue of relocation cost claims has been fully resolved, beginning with the 2025 permanent appointment cohort.
"The Health Ministry has also secured approval for the same benefit to continue for 2026 appointments and beyond," it said.
The clarification follows social media posts claiming that some doctors were facing difficulties reporting for duty in Sabah and Sarawak after allegedly being denied the right to claim relocation costs.
The ministry said the benefit was also in line with the 20 Madani Government Initiatives for the Welfare of Health Ministry Personnel, under which officers who are converted to permanent status are eligible to claim the full relocation allowance.
Meanwhile, the ministry said the shortage of doctors and uneven distribution of medical officers at health facilities could be addressed after it was given autonomy by PSD to manage and distribute posts.
"Through this important step, the issue can be reduced in stages.
"The government has also taken several long-term measures, including offering permanent appointments to 4,500 contract medical officers this year," it said.
In addition, the ministry has required contract medical officers who receive permanent appointments to choose at least one posting in Sabah, Sarawak or Labuan through improvements to the ePlacement system, beginning last year.
"This initiative is aimed at addressing doctor shortages in certain areas.
"Meanwhile, the waiting period for placement in the medical graduate training programme has also been shortened to two months from more than 10 months previously," it said.
The implementation of the 20 Madani Government Initiatives for the Welfare of Health Ministry Personnel 2026 will also continue to be strengthened to safeguard the welfare, career security and working environment of the country's health workers.
"Among them is the phasing out of the contract doctor system, with contract doctors to be absorbed into permanent positions in stages by 2028.
"In addition, 18,755 permanent positions covering medical, pharmacy and dental officers have been filled," it said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Anti-vax posts weaponise Philippine inoculation fears
Article:
WHEN Jenette Torres Odena's 3-year-old son fell ill days after receiving a jab as part of a Philippine vaccination drive, his photograph  spread on Facebook alongside claims the inoculation had killed him.
Doctors found no link between the boy's condition and the measles-rubella vaccine, and he went on to fully recover, but by then his image had appeared in anti-vaccine videos viewed hundreds of thousands of times.
"I felt like crying," Odena said. "I kept praying for my son to recover, and suddenly, they were killing him on Facebook."
The videos were part of a wave of misinformation that accompanied a child vaccination campaign this year that saw more than seven million Filipinos inoculated. Some 230,000 declined the jab.
The Department of Health said concerns about side effects accounted for 66 per cent of refusals and called misinformation spread by social media influencers a "major driver" of vaccine fear.
The Philippines has struggled to restore routine childhood immunisation rates after years of plummeting coverage, which contributed to a polio resurgence in 2019 and recurring measles outbreaks.
The claims circulated on social media recycled conspiracy theories that gained traction during the Covid-19 pandemic while tapping into lingering fears about vaccine safety after the botched rollout of a dengue vaccine in the Philippines a decade ago.
"Vaccine hesitancy should not simply be understood as a lack of scientific knowledge among the public," saod Daniel Fritz Silvallana, a health communication researcher at Deakin University, Australia.
"In the Philippine context, it is also connected to questions of trust, politics and people's previous experiences with vaccination and public health institutions."
Within days of the photo of Odena's son being shared online, Facebook content creator Maharani Sona Shiloh had incorporated it into a video, framing it as evidence the vaccination campaign was harming children.
To bolster her claims, Shiloh cited Trump's recent controversial move to reduce the number of vaccine doses administered to American children.
The video viewed hundreds of thousands of times paired the child's image with a photograph of US President Donald Trump and the words "Everyday slaughter".
Facebook eventually took down the page. Three affiliated pages remain active.
Shiloh rejected suggestions she was spreading harmful misinformation, describing herself as a human rights advocate.
The 44-year-old said she became involved in anti-vaccine advocacy years before the pandemic, later connecting with church groups and "advocacy circles" that also campaign against SIM card registration and other policies they associate with a treacherous "New World Order".
Videos posted by Shiloh, some with millions of views, claimed vaccines contained harmful substances, including "human placenta" and "formalin", while warning that the World Health Organisation was trying to depopulate the planet.
One mother, who asked to speak anonymously to protect her children, said  she decided to hold off on vaccinating them after watching the videos.
A week after the Facebook page was shuttered, she said she remained undecided about vaccinating her children, explaining that she and her husband worried about possible side effects.
While Shiloh's claims quickly collapse under scientific scrutiny, vaccinologist Helen Petousis-Harris of the University of Auckland said these videos rely on fear rather than compelling evidence.
"Recognised vaccine ingredients become mysterious contaminants. Rare adverse events become brain damage, epilepsy organ failure and death."
For health workers on the frontlines, however, the videos are increasingly difficult to ignore.
"They get scared because the vlog said vaccines are fatal," said Wenna Mae Belen, a rural health worker in Sorsogon province.
"They tell me if something bad happens, they'll make me suck the vaccines out of their kids' bodies."
While Facebook bore "major responsibility" for the spread of vaccine misinformation, she said  picking fights with content creators like Shiloh and their followers was a losing battle.
Rebuilding trust will take time and patience, she said, calling for open, non-judgmental conversations with parents.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: America's war machine needs a reload
Article:
AS America's military cyberdefence professionals met for their annual trade meeting in Maryland last Thursday, top commanders issued a blunt warning that sustained operations this year had cost the United States much of its long-built-up advantages in cyberspace.
According to US officials, highly sophisticated cyberattacks were at the heart of operations earlier this year, firstly to capture Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro and then to degrade Iranian sensors and communications in the US-led Operation Epic Fury.
Over time, however, senior officials told the gathering of the Military Cyber Professionals Association, known as Hammercon, their ability to conduct offensive cyberattacks through pre-identified vulnerabilities in hostile systems has begun eroding fast.
"Your cyber magazine of these exquisite fires is empty pretty damn quick," Vice-Admiral Heidi Berg, commander of the US Navy Fleet Cyber Command, said in response to a question, referring to the abilities to hack and frustrate or turn off key systems in an opposing nation.
According to Lieutenant-General Christopher Eubank, head of US Army Cyber Command speaking at the same event, demand for direct US cyber support to wider military operations had been "constant" since the conflict with Iran began on Feb 28.
He said this was the "first time for the cyber force at large" that operations have been at such a tempo.
Those lessons in cyberspace appear to overlap heavily with much wider trend,  particularly the overuse of precision missiles, including those for air defence.
Multiple US military sources told Reuters the Pentagon had used up large stockpiles of ATACMS strike missiles, Patriot air defence systems and Tomahawk long-range cruise missiles, to the point that it would take multiple years to rebuild "magazine depth".
The strain has also been telling on other parts of the US military.
Last week, US Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao confirmed that eight sailors aboard the USS
Abraham Lincoln
aircraft carrier had attempted suicide during
its unusually long 286 consecutive days at sea this year supporting operations in the Middle East.
Events this year have acted as a savage and robust reminder of US military strength.
They have shown the stark limits of that power and the damage to the US military inventory goes well beyond just the used up missile stocks.
According to US specialist defence media reports, the US Air Force has lost as many as 40 of its MQ-9 Reaper drones in its operations since the end of February, as much as a quarter of its total airworthy fleet.
Other aircraft losses have also been on a scale unseen in recent US wars, including two KC-135 tankers destroyed and another seven damaged, a wrecked E-3 Sentry airborne warning aircraft, four destroyed F-15E Strike Eagles and another eight damaged.
Two MC-130J gunships and an A-10 Warthog were also lost on a mission to retrieve a downed pilot.
Still, estimates from the Congressional Budget Office put the financial expense of Operation Epic Fury so far as just under US$40 billion, pointedly warning it would take several years to rebuild depleted stocks of interceptor missiles critical for deterring any future war with China.
This week, US military publication
Stars and Stripes
noted that the US was moving to store long-range Typhon and High Mobility Artillery Rocket System missiles at Kadena Air Force Base in Okinawa.
That move was announced jointly with Japan and likely intended to reassure US regional allies and remind Beijing that, despite a largely friendly meeting between US President Donald Trump and China's Xi Jinping, the US remains ready to fight a war if needed.
When it comes to supporting allies this year, the US record has been distinctly mixed — with Saudi Arabia, in particular, now turning to wider foreign help despite the presence of what Gulf media say have been more than 100 US advisers on the ground.
According to French President Emmanuel Macron, French troops and missiles are now helping protect the Saudi port of Yanbu, while Riyadh is  publicly discussing further support with treaty allies Pakistan and Turkiye.
Russian missiles, meanwhile, continue to pound Ukrainian targets, now helped by a lack of US-manufactured interceptors.
A broader realisation is that launching conflict is much easier to do than managing the resulting fallout.
The writer is from Reuters

Title: NST Leader: Zetrix RM200m revenue lapse exposes urgent need for stronger RTD oversight'
Article:
THE revelation that Zetrix AI Bhd, formerly known as MyEG Sdn Bhd, owes the Road Transport Department (RTD) more than RM200 million in unremitted collections is shocking.
The e-government services pioneer, which has operated since 2000, collected payments on behalf of the Road Transport Department (RTD) for road tax, driving licences and traffic summonses.
Zetrix, which assumed its new name in July last year 2025, reportedly failed to remit the fees it collected from the start of its three-year contract in May 2023. Why did Zetrix stop remitting the money? We do not know, but its financial position raises questions.
Corporate disclosures and media reports show that its development expenditure rose sharply to more than RM3.7 billion, while it also faced substantial debt obligations. Still, motorists have not been left without options, as RTD JPJ has directed them to its official and alternative payment channels.
Now comes the crunch. The Zetrix issue raises serious questions about RTD's financial controls, monitoring and accountability. It is no longer just about the money, but how the situation was allowed to persist without earlier intervention.
The obvious questions are: what safeguards were in place and, if they existed, why did they fail?
What were Zetrix's contractual obligations for remitting the collections? Are collections reconciled daily, weekly or monthly with RTD's records?
Are there automatic alerts when payments are overdue, independent audits and clear escalation procedures?
Were there earlier warnings, discrepancies, demands for payment or breaches of contractual obligations? If there were warnings, why was stronger action not taken earlier?
Agencies that appoint private firms to collect funds on behalf of the government must have robust systems to ensure prompt and accurate remittance. If such controls existed, RTD has some explaining to do: Why was there a lapse in compliance?, AND Why were the arrears allowed to accumulate?
Accountability must extend beyond recovering the more than RM200 million. The government needs to establish exactly how the arrears were allowed to build up, whether existing monitoring systems failed, and what safeguards are needed to prevent a similar situation involving public collections from happening again.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Three arrested after entering Kelantan through illegal jetty
Article:
RANTAU PANJANG: A man and two women who had just returned from an entertainment trip in Sungai Golok were arrested after entering Kelantan through an illegal jetty here yesterday.
Southeast Brigade General Operations Force commander Datuk Ahmad Radzi Hussain said the three Malaysians were arrested by a team from its Eighth Battalion about 7.30pm.
He said the trio, aged 18, 20 and 32, had just crossed the Golok River by boat when they were detained at the Abe Yie illegal jetty.
"The three admitted they had visited an entertainment centre in Sungai Golok town.
"They also admitted to taking drugs while at the entertainment centre," he said.
Radzi said urine tests on the 20-year-old and 18-year-old women returned positive for methamphetamine.
"The 32-year-old man tested negative. All three were from Kelantan," he added.
He said the three were arrested for entering Malaysia through an unauthorised route under Section 5(2) of the Immigration Act 1959/63.
"The case has been handed over to the Pasir Mas police station," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Daughter finds 85-year-old mother dead in bushes behind house
Article:
BACHOK: An 85-year-old woman was found dead in bushes behind her house in Kampung Pengkalan Baru here this afternoon.
The victim, Che Bidah Sulung, was found by her eldest daughter, Hilmiah Hamzah, in her 60s, who had gone to the house to deliver food.
Another daughter, Hindun Hamzah, 58, said she was informed of the incident about 3pm.
"Mother lived alone in the house. It was a routine for her children and nieces to send her food every day.
"Earlier, my sister called me to say she was going to send rice to mother's house. However, mother was not there.
"She searched around the house before finding mother unresponsive in the bushes behind the house," she said when met at the scene today.
Hindun said her mother was active and enjoyed cleaning around the house.
She said the family believed Che Bidah could have been behind the house to clean the area.
Hindun said her mother also had no known illnesses and the family was still shocked by the incident.
Meanwhile, Bachok district police chief Superintendent Mohamad Ismail Jamaluddin confirmed receiving a report on the incident.
He said the woman's body was taken to Bachok Hospital for further action and investigations would be carried out to determine the cause of death.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Malaysia welcomes Bahrain investment, seeks wider cooperation, says Anwar
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia welcomes investment from Bahrain and is ready to expand cooperation in various fields, Prime Minister Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim said.
In a social media post tonight, Anwar said the cooperation would cover healthcare, Islamic finance, technology, tourism, food security, artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity and smart manufacturing.
He said these were among the areas discussed during his meeting with Bahrain's Crown Prince and Prime Minister Prince Salman bin Hamad Al-Khalifa, who is visiting Malaysia in conjunction with the 2026 Formula 1 (F1) Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix in Malaysia.

Title: Two hikers rescued after getting lost in Penang forest
Article:
GEORGE TOWN: Two hikers were safely rescued after getting lost in the forest near Taman Belia, Botanical Garden, tonight.
Penang Fire and Rescue Department assistant operations director John Sagun Francis said the department received an emergency call at 6.11pm.

Title: 'I didn't distance myself without reason': Ex-PJ MP on PKR exit
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Former Petaling Jaya member of parliament Lee Chean Chung has rejected claims that he was absent from PKR affairs for more than a year, saying he became less active after an alleged corporate mafia issue he raised within the party was not acted upon.
Lee, who announced his resignation as Petaling Jaya MP yesterday, said the claim that he had been "missing for more than a year" from party affairs was inaccurate and diverted attention from the reason for his reduced involvement.
"My statement that I was 'missing for more than a year' from party affairs is inaccurate. It diverts attention from the root cause of this situation.
"I did not distance myself without reason. I became less active after the corporate mafia issue I raised through internal channels was ignored," he said in a Facebook post today.
Yesterday, Lee announced his resignation as Petaling Jaya MP with immediate effect, following his three-year suspension from PKR.
He said the decision followed his receipt of the suspension decision on Sept 30. He also claimed that access to RM3 million in allocations for the Petaling Jaya constituency had previously been blocked and the funds placed under the management of a party representative.
PKR president Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim subsequently said the party had no issue with Lee's resignation, adding that the former MP had not attended PKR meetings or congresses for more than a year.
Lee also questioned PKR's handling of his complaints concerning an alleged corporate mafia, following businessman Victor Chin's allegation that a PKR MP had received RM9.5 million to "settle" a corporate mafia issue involving him.
Lee said such a serious allegation against an elected representative from the ruling party should have been investigated promptly and transparently.
"To this day, no action has been taken. Instead, I, who pushed for the issue to be investigated, was the one who was restricted and punished.
"On Jan 26, I called for an investigation into the issue of excessive shareholdings involving Tan Sri Azam Baki and the corporate mafia issue in Parliament. No action was taken.
"In April, I met the prime minister and sought a Royal Commission of Inquiry (RCI). No action was taken.
"On May 26, my constituency allocation was blocked and handed to a political party to manage. On June 12, I resigned as a member of the PKR Central Leadership Council (MPP).
"On July 2, I received a show-cause letter from the PKR Disciplinary Board. I responded on July 9 but received no reply.
"Then, on Aug 20, I personally wrote to the Disciplinary Board and requested a hearing so that I could defend myself. The request was ignored," he said.
Lee questioned the disciplinary action taken against him after he raised the issues.
"Why was the MP who called for an investigation punished, while the MP accused of receiving RM9.5 million was not investigated?
"Malaysians cannot compromise the country's reputation in the eyes of the international community.
"We cannot be seen as compromising in the fight against corruption, especially under a government elected on a reform mandate," he said.
Lee said the fundamental issue was not who was active or inactive, but why reported misconduct had not been investigated while those who exposed it were punished.
"I remain committed to the people of Petaling Jaya and to the principles that brought me into politics — integrity, accountability and the courage to speak up even when it is unpopular," he said.
